claims.text: The infant’s current CRP trend (19 mg/L at 4 h, 10 mg/L at 8 h) is decreasing but remains above normal; a single falling value does not exclude early‑onset sepsis.

Because the blood culture is still pending and the initial clinical suspicion is not strong, antibiotics can be stopped at 36 h if the infant remains clinically reassuring and CRP trends are reassuring.
Continue monitoring vital signs and clinical status for at least 12 h using a newborn early warning system before deciding to stop antibiotics.
If the infant develops any new clinical indicators of infection or CRP rises, antibiotics should be restarted and the infant reassessed within 24 h.
Obtain a repeat CRP and repeat blood culture at 36 h to inform the decision to stop or continue antibiotics.
Explain to parents that a single falling CRP does not rule out sepsis and that antibiotic therapy will be reviewed at 36 h based on clinical and laboratory trends.

packet.evaluation_question: Can a single or falling CRP result exclude early-onset sepsis or alone determine whether antibiotics stop? Explain the limits of inflammatory markers. Gestation 41 weeks; age 12 hours; setting postnatal ward.

evidence.text: If continuing antibiotics for longer than 48 hours for suspected late‑onset neonatal infection despite negative blood culture, review the baby at least once every 24 hours. At each review, decide whether to stop antibiotics, taking account of: • the level of initial clinical suspicion of infection and • the baby's clinical progress and current condition and • the levels and trends of C-reactive protein. [2021]

For babies born from 35+0 weeks' gestation with negative blood culture who need antibiotics for more than 36 hours because the initial clinical suspicion of infection was strong, consider switching treatment from intravenous to oral antibiotics at 36 hours or thereafter to complete the course (up to 7 days of antibiotics in total) if: • the baby's clinical condition is reassuring, with no current clinical indicators of ongoing infection (see box 2 for clinical indicators of possible early-onset neonatal infection) and • the levels and trends of C-reactive protein concentration are reassuring and • the baby is tolerating oral feeds. [2026]

For babies who are being treated with intravenous antibiotics because of risk factors for early-onset infection or clinical indicators of possible infection, stop antibiotics at 36 hours if: • the blood culture is negative and • the initial clinical suspicion of infection was not strong and • the baby's clinical condition is reassuring, with no clinical indicators of possible infection (see box 2 for clinical indicators of possible early-onset infection) and • the levels and trends of C-reactive protein concentration are reassuring. [2012, amended 2026]

Use the following framework, based on the risk factors in box 1 and the clinical indicators in box 2, to make antibiotic management decisions as directed: • In babies with any red flag, or with 2 or more 'non-red-flag' risk factors or clinical indicators: － follow the recommendations in the section on investigations before starting antibiotics and － start antibiotic treatment according to the recommendations in this guideline and － do not wait for the test results before starting antibiotics • in babies without red flags and only 1 risk factor or 1 clinical indicator, use clinical judgement to decide: － whether it is safe to withhold antibiotics and － whether the baby's vital signs and clinical condition need to be monitored. If monitoring is needed, continue for at least 12 hours using a newborn early warning system • for babies without risk factors or clinical indicators of possible infection, continue routine postnatal care as covered in NICE's guideline on postnatal care. [2021]
